_comment: Speeds are pixels per simulation tick; multiply by 60 for pixels per second.
A tile is 16 pixels, so 1.7 is about six and a half tiles a second.
Every enemy is slower than every class. That is the deal the whole fight
rests on: you can always disengage, so getting hit is a decision you made
rather than something the arena did to you. The binding number is the
Knight's 1.45 -- the slowest thing the player can be -- so nothing hostile
may exceed it, and a test enforces that against the slowest class rather
than against an average.
aggro is in pixels -- how far an enemy notices you from.
_class_comment: The five playable classes, in the order the character select shows them.
Anything with faction 'hero' is offered to the player, so this list is the
roster -- there is no second place to register a class.
They are separated by what they ask of you, not by a power level:
Knight    -- can you afford to commit? Slowest, toughest, hits hardest.
Rogue     -- can you stay in? Fragile, fastest, no swing costs anything.
Archer    -- can you keep the room between you? Ranged, average at all else.
Magician  -- can you find the gap? Long commitment, biggest single hit.
Priest    -- can you last? Middling everywhere, recovers twice as much.
heal_between_stages is the class's own dial, not a global one, and every
one of the five was measured separately rather than scaled from a single
number. Scaling was tried first and does not work: what a class needs back
between stages depends on how much damage it takes to clear one, and that
varies by more than its health pool does. On a median stage the Rogue and
the Archer spend about 17% of their bar, the Knight 27%, the Priest 30% --
so the Priest needs the largest heal as a fraction and the Rogue one of the
smallest, which is the opposite of what the health pools suggest.
That is also where the Priest's identity lives. Sixty-two of ninety-five is
two thirds of the bar back after every stage; nobody else clears half. It
is a run-level answer to a run-level problem, which is why the class looks
so ordinary on any single stage.
Rerun tools/balance.py --class all after touching any of these. They are
measured numbers and they do not survive being guessed at.

knight.name: Knight
_comment: The reference class -- the one the campaign is measured against, and the
default everywhere a class is not named. Most health, most damage, worst
mobility: the slowest roll on the longest cooldown, so disengaging is a
thing the Knight plans rather than a thing it does.

rogue.name: Rogue
_comment: Fastest body and fastest roll on the shortest cooldown. Eighty health is
about three hits from an act boss, so the mobility is not a luxury -- it
is the only defence the class has.

archer.name: Archer
_comment: Fights at the range the enemy archers want to, and wins that trade -- a
faster arrow and a much shorter windup. The catch is that a shot spends
itself on the first thing it touches, so the pillars that keep bowmen off
you also eat your damage, and a room full of rats closes the distance the
whole class depends on.

magician.name: Magician
_comment: The longest commitment of any class, on a body that cannot afford it.
Thirty-one ticks per bolt means every shot is a decision about the next
half second. Started at 75 health and lost six stages of the campaign
outright -- a class that commits for that long needs to survive being
wrong about it. The longest iframes in the game for the same reason.

priest.name: Priest
_comment: Unremarkable in a fight and hard to finish off across a campaign. Forty
health back between stages is more than twice anyone else, which makes a
badly cleared stage recoverable rather than a debt carried into the next
act. The class is a run-level answer to a run-level problem, which is why
it looks so ordinary on any single stage.

_enemy_comment: Anything with faction 'enemy'. Brains are code (game/ai.py), not data --
'chaser', 'charger', 'archer' and 'boss' are the four that exist, and two
different creatures sharing one is normal. The 'archer' brain in particular
describes a behaviour (keep your distance, need line of sight) rather than
a creature: both the bowman and the mage use it.

grunt.name: Grunt
grunt._comment: Straightforward pressure. Walks at you, swings when close.

rat.name: Rat
_comment: Dies to one hit from anything and is barely slower than you, so it cannot
be outrun the way a grunt can -- it has to be dealt with. Individually
trivial and collectively the reason the second act is about crowd control
rather than about any one enemy.
Also the honest test of a ranged class: a rat closes the distance an
Archer or Magician is built around, and there are always more of them.

charger.name: Charger
_comment: Slow until it commits, then faster than you. Punishes standing in a line
with it. The long windup on 'gore' is the tell you dodge on.

brute.name: Brute
_comment: The slowest thing in the game that is not a boss, and the hardest hitting
thing that is not one either. Alone it is free damage -- you can walk away
from it indefinitely. The point of a brute is that it makes every other
enemy in the room more dangerous, because none of them let you spend the
time it takes to kill it.

bowman.name: Bowman
bowman._comment: Punishes standing still in the open. Backs away when you close.

mage.name: Mage
_comment: A bowman that stands further back and hurts much more. The hex is slow
enough to walk out of, so it costs you position rather than health -- and
position is what the third act keeps asking for.

_boss_comment: One boss ends each act: stages 5, 10, 15 and 20.
All four share the 'boss' brain, which is positional about its weapons --
weapons[0] is the sweep it uses up close, weapons[1] is the charge it uses
at mid range, weapons[2] is what it shoots from far away. Declare them in
any other order and it will telegraph one attack and land another. A test
enforces the ordering.
sprite_scale 2 is not decoration: render/hud.py decides what gets a boss
health bar by looking for it. A boss without it fights normally and shows
no bar.
Below half health every one of them stops pausing between attacks (see
game/ai.py). That is the whole phase system -- no new moves to learn at the
moment you are least able to learn them, just less room to breathe.
**On why the later bosses are not much tougher than the first.** There is
no progression in this game: the Knight that fights the Sovereign on stage
20 swings exactly the greatsword it had on stage 1. So health on a boss buys
fight *length* and nothing else -- and a fight twice as long against the same
moveset is not twice as interesting, it is the same fight with more chances
to make the one mistake that ends it.
This was measured rather than reasoned about. The Effigy started at 240 and
the Sovereign at 280, and both were unwinnable on every seed: not close,
not a tuning pass away -- the hero simply ran out of health partway down the
bar. What makes each of these harder than the Warden is the cadence, the
reach and the size of the arena, which is where a later boss should be
getting its difficulty from anyway.

boss.name: The Warden
_comment: End of act one, and the fight that teaches the pattern the other three
vary. Slower than anything else and much harder to kill, so it lasts long
enough for its three attacks to become something you read rather than
three things that happen to you.
aggro covers the whole arena -- there is no sneaking up on it, and no
corner it forgets about you in.

houndmaster.name: The Houndmaster
_comment: End of act two. Less health than the Warden and half again its speed --
the same three questions asked in a hurry. It closes the distance a ranged
class wants, and the shorter telegraphs mean the answers you learned on
stage five have to come faster rather than differently.

effigy.name: The Effigy
_comment: End of act three, and the opposite reading of the Warden: slower than
anything in the game, with the longest tells and the largest numbers.
Nothing it does is hard to see coming. The fight is long enough that the
question is whether you can keep answering correctly for two minutes, not
whether you can answer at all.

sovereign.name: The Sovereign
_comment: The last fight. Deliberately nothing new -- the same three attacks in the
same three positions the Warden used fifteen stages earlier, with every
number raised and none of the room. Everything the player learned still
applies, which is the point of ending on it rather than on a fourth idea.
aggro of 700 covers any arena it could be placed in.
